voice_event.text: To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is: the eternal Son of God, crucified under Pontius Pilate, risen the third day, ascended to the Father's right hand. That was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. We held the ancient creeds as our own. What we contested was not who he is, but how his body is given at the Supper and who finally decides who belongs to him. What is distinctly ours is what we were taught about who is chosen in him. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned. We hold that as a settled ground, not a threat. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and rejected looking for that apart from him. What we actually have of him is not a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms.

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text: He lived without sin, bore the punishment our own sin earned, died on the cross as the one sufficient sacrifice for all who would ever believe, and rose bodily on the third day. That is what the whole church has always confessed, and we confessed it with them. What we contested was not what he did, but how that finished work reaches us now. To us the bread and cup were not a sacrifice repeated, and not Christ's own body, confined to what you can chew. Our own founder said this first: the mass is a remembrance, not a sacrifice. Twenty-six years later, both our cities spoke together on the same Supper. We distinguished the sign from what it points to, but we did not pull them apart: all who take the promise in faith receive Christ spiritually. What he did was done once, and it does not need doing again. What reaches us at the table is not a new sacrifice but the one sacrifice, truly given by the Spirit to whoever receives him believing.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text: Providence. It is God's own continuous, active care over everything he made. He is not a distant first cause who set the world going and stepped back. The word comes from Latin providentia, seeing beforehand. We used it to name the way God governs what he created, moment by moment, without pause. It answers a question someone might press on us: if God chose who would be saved before the world began, does anything anyone does actually matter? We said it does, because providence is not fate. God does not merely know what will happen and let it unfold on its own. He actively sustains and directs it. This doctrine stood alongside election as part of how we taught God's own sovereignty. Both Zurich and Geneva held it. Geneva's Calvin worked it into a full system. Zurich's founders stated it more briefly, and pastorally. The word itself was not ours alone - the whole church had always used it - but we meant by it what I have said: not distant decree but active, unceasing care.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text: We believed it because Scripture itself taught us that God's choice came first, not ours. God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. Both Zurich and Geneva held this. Not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen - not a future faith God looked ahead and saw, not a worthiness he detected before the world existed - but his own free choice alone. We held that as a settled ground, not a threat. The reason we held it was that it put the whole weight of our standing before God on God himself, not on us. If our salvation rested on anything we contributed, even the faith that receives it, we would have reason to wonder whether we had contributed enough. This doctrine answered that question before it could be asked. It also answered the pastoral weight of doubt. In 1551, a man named Jerome Bolsec stood up at Geneva and challenged this teaching directly. It became a live crisis, not a settled doctrine everyone already accepted. We held it because we believed it was what the text actually said, and because it was the only ground we could stand on without looking to ourselves.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text: Our pastor at Geneva, John Calvin, lived it. He arrived the same year Geneva broke from Savoy and the Prince-Bishop, 1536. He was exiled to Strasbourg three years later, then recalled in 1541 to consolidate what became the Ecclesiastical Ordinances. That document is the root of Geneva's own Consistory and its disciplinary independence. He built the doctrine we held into a full, systematic form. His Institutes worked it out article by article until the whole shape stood complete. He also traveled to Zurich in 1549 with Farel, when others doubted that Geneva's teaching and Zurich's agreed on the Supper. That meeting became the Consensus Tigurinus. What I cannot give you is the texture of his ordinary days, or how his own teaching felt to someone who heard it week by week. Our record does not hold that.

voice_event.text: That we refused as much as we confessed. Ask what we are, and part of the true answer is what we refused. We refused Rome: no repeated sacrifice, no image bowed to, because Scripture does not warrant either. We refused Wittenberg, once the question was pressed at Marburg: no claim that Christ's own body is confined to the bread. And we refused a third claim from inside our own circle at Zurich. It said the church must be gathered only by a believer's own profession, apart from the whole city. It came from men who had once stood with our own founder before they broke from him. We do not call these three refusals the same kind of act. One answered an order we inherited. One resisted a rival still pressing from outside. One was a wound from within, and it was the sharpest because it came from our own. Nor will we tell you it was answered only with argument. Our own council turned to civil force against that third refusal in the years that followed, and our own record does not hide that.
